history.heading: Isthmus of the Americas
paragraphs: Panama, the narrow isthmus linking North and South America, was home to indigenous peoples such as the Guna, Emberá and Ngäbe. Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed it in 1513, becoming the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas.

Panama City, founded in 1519, became a key route for transporting Peruvian silver and gold to Spain. The pirate Henry Morgan sacked it in 1671. Its ruins (Panamá Viejo) and the Caribbean forts of Portobelo are UNESCO sites.

history.heading: Colombia and the canal
paragraphs: Panama became independent from Spain in 1821 as part of Gran Colombia and later Colombia. A French attempt to build a canal in the 1880s failed. In 1903, with US support, Panama separated from Colombia, and the United States gained control of a Canal Zone. The Panama Canal opened in 1914.

US control of the zone caused tensions, including deadly riots in 1964. The Torrijos–Carter Treaties of 1977 arranged the canal's handover, completed on 31 December 1999. In 1989 the United States invaded Panama to remove military ruler Manuel Noriega.

culture.heading: A crossroads culture
paragraphs: Spanish is the official language. Panama's population is mainly mestizo, with Afro-Panamanian, indigenous and immigrant communities. Most people are Catholic. Guna women's colourful molas (textile panels) are famous.

The pollera, an elaborate embroidered dress, is the national costume. Sancocho (chicken soup) is the national dish. Baseball and boxing are popular, and salsa singer Rubén Blades is internationally known.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Panama is a presidential republic with a president elected for five years and a unicameral National Assembly. José Raúl Mulino became president in 2024. In 2025 US claims about Chinese influence over the canal created tensions, and Panama withdrew from China's Belt and Road Initiative. Large protests in 2023 led to the closure of a major copper mine.

economy.heading: Services and the canal
paragraphs: Panama has one of the fastest-growing economies in Latin America over recent decades. The Panama Canal, expanded in 2016, is a vital route for world trade and a major source of revenue; droughts in 2023–24 restricted traffic. Banking, logistics, the Colón Free Trade Zone, ship registration (one of the world's largest) and tourism are key sectors.
Panama uses the US dollar alongside the balboa. Inequality remains high.
